sections.html:
Across the water from Louisville, Clark County stretches back from the Indiana bank of the Ohio. Jeffersonville is the seat and the biggest city, and Clarksville, Charlestown, Sellersburg, Henryville, Marysville and Speed turn up on deeds all the time. The 2020 census put the county at 121,093 residents and Jeffersonville at 49,447, a jump driven partly by annexation.

Annexation shows up on the bill. Neighboring streets can fall under different taxing units, and each statement adds county, city and school levies into a single total, so check your parcel's district before comparing numbers with a friend.

Buyers raise water and wind early. March 2012 tornadoes tore through Marysville and Henryville, so a house in those towns may be a rebuild, and inspectors ask for permits and repair receipts. Close to the Ohio or a creek, expect flood-coverage questions, and keep any elevation or damage papers in one folder.

Inside Jeffersonville, a parcel may sit in Port Fulton, the historic area where the Howard Shipyards once stood, in Oak Park, annexed in 2008, or near the downtown riverfront around Big Four Station. Each pocket has its own crowd. The Big Four Bridge, a former rail span that now carries walkers and cyclists, has turned the riverfront into a draw.

Jobs steer demand. River Ridge occupies the old Indiana Army Ammunition Plant grounds and hosts makers of aerospace, automotive, food and beverage goods, plus life sciences and logistics firms. Since the 1950s, Interstate 65 has pulled subdivisions and shopping centers outward. The Jeffboat yard shut in 2018, and an 80-acre riverfront site is slated for redevelopment. Staff at Norton Clark Hospital, the schools and the Census Bureau's processing center rent and buy nearby, which matters if you own a rental.

The yearly total splits into a spring half and a fall half. Look for May 10 and November 10, with paper bills arriving in early April. Copy A is the spring stub and Copy B is the fall stub, and a weekend due date slides to the next business day.

The treasurer's counter is at 300 Corporate Drive, Suite 105, Jeffersonville, and the line is 812-285-6205. Staff are there weekdays from 8:30 a.m. until 4:30 p.m. but step away from noon to 1 p.m. By mail, enclose the matching stub plus a stamped return envelope addressed to yourself, and send it to PO Box 1689, Evansville, IN 47706 for a receipt.

A few local banks also accept payments during collection season, as long as you show the bill, owe nothing delinquent, and pay on time.

To contest a value, hand the assessor a Form 130 for each parcel. June 15 is the line, counted in the year the notice (Form 11) goes out, or in the year the bill is mailed if no notice was sent. Your notice shows the date that applies.

An informal sit-down with the assessor comes first, and the result goes to the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals. The formal hearing is due within 180 days, with 30 days of mailed warning. Missing it, unless you asked for a continuance or withdrew, can bring a $50 charge. If the board ruling stands against you, the next stop is the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131.

Bring proof to the meeting: closed sales of similar houses, an appraisal, or photos and contractor quotes for repairs. A tidy folder persuades better than a feeling that the figure is too high.

Delinquent parcels are put up at a tax certificate sale that the Clark County Treasurer conducts. Whoever wins holds a lien, evidenced by a Tax Sale Certificate that the County Auditor issues.

Redemption stays open for twelve months after the sale, if the owner pays the Indiana Code amounts with interest. Without redemption, the bidder may petition for a tax deed. Listings appear at sriservices.com. Get legal advice if your parcel is on the list.

Earlier in the process, a payment made within 30 days of the due date carries a 5% penalty if the parcel was current before. Any other late payment carries 10%. Selling a house that is heading toward the list can stop the balance from growing.

sections.h2: Selling a Clark County house with taxes due
sections.html:
Worn-out houses, inherited homes and tired landlords make up most quick sales here, and each raises tax questions. Run down this list:

  • Call the treasurer for the current balance before you set a closing date.
  • Complete the state sales disclosure form, which must be done before the deed reaches the auditor.
  • Gather permits and storm repair records if the house is by the river or in a tornado zone.
  • If you took the homestead deduction, the new owner who closes after the assessment date may claim it by December 31 of the purchase year.

Owing tax does not block a sale. The balance is subtracted from what you receive at the table. Selling for cash spares you showings and repair work, though the tax settles the same way.

Two habits prevent headaches. Ask the treasurer to put the payoff in writing and pass it to your closer. Also hold on to the bill, because the office wants a stub with any payment and charges $1.00 per parcel for a duplicate. If a due date slips by before closing, a 5% or 10% penalty can attach.

An inherited house may still be billed in the name of the late owner. Bring the estate papers to the treasurer and the closer early, and update the mailing address so notices reach whoever manages the sale. A tenant changes nothing about the due dates, so fold the next installment into your closing numbers.

A workable timeline: week one, phone the treasurer for the balance, pull the deed history and decide on repairs. Week two, gather offers and choose a closer. Just before signing, ask for the payoff again, since penalties and payment dates move the figure. On closing day the agent pays the tax, records the deed and cuts your check. Keep each receipt in one folder in case a buyer's lender wants proof.

One more point for landlords and heirs: a house that has sat vacant often has a tax history nobody has looked at in years. Before you list, ask the treasurer whether any earlier year is open, since a parcel with an old balance is the one that ends up on the tax sale list. Finding that out early gives you room to pay it or to price the sale around it.

faqs.q: When do Clark County property taxes come due?
faqs.a: Usually May 10 and November 10. Copy A is the spring stub, Copy B the fall one, and bills typically mail in early April.

faqs.q: Where do I pay in person in Clark County?
faqs.a: At the treasurer's counter, 300 Corporate Drive, Suite 105, Jeffersonville. It is open weekdays and shuts for the noon hour. Mailed payments go to PO Box 1689, Evansville, IN 47706.

faqs.q: How long can I redeem after a Clark County tax sale?
faqs.a: Twelve months from the sale date. After that the bidder may petition for a tax deed, and redeeming means paying the statutory amounts plus interest.

faqs.q: What is the Clark County appeal deadline?
faqs.a: June 15 in the year your Form 11 or tax bill is mailed. File Form 130, one per parcel, and read your own notice for the exact date.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Clark County house that has back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. Your closer subtracts the balance from the proceeds. Ask the treasurer for a payoff first, since a 5% or 10% penalty may apply.
